episode.throughLine: A young sculptor tells a contemporary writer how she sought advice and asks for useful criticism instead of praise based on her race.

contentProfile.contentNote: Short reported-conversation vignette. Racially condescending praise, without slurs or the former assault and poisoning narrative. The focus is learning and requesting useful criticism; no completed studio visit or improvement is claimed.

sources.citation: Lydia Maria Child, Letter from L. Maria Child, The Liberator, 19 February 1864.

facts.statement: Child reported meeting Lewis at a reception and speaking with her about becoming a sculptor.

sourceRefs.locator: p31 column3, paragraph One of the most interesting individuals.

facts.statement: Lewis told Child that her brother brought her to Boston to learn sculpture and that she sought Brackett's advice, considering his John Brown bust a reason to expect sympathy.

sourceRefs.locator: p31 column3, answer beginning I have a brother through Mr. Brackett has been very kind.

facts.statement: Lewis told Child that Brackett had treated her kindly.

sourceRefs.locator: p31 column3, end of answer beginning I have a brother.

facts.statement: Child reported that Lewis wanted her to visit her room to see her first bust, copied from a head of Voltaire.

sourceRefs.locator: p31 column3, paragraph She wanted me, opening sentence.

facts.statement: Lewis told Child that praise was not good for her, did not want praise because of her race and wanted defects identified so she could learn.

sourceRefs.locator: p31 column3, paragraph She wanted me, quoted request from I don't want through teach me something.

facts.statement: Edmonia Lewis was a sculptor who made marble portraits.

sourceRefs.locator: Artist/Maker, Medium, and More Information paragraphs3–5.

dramatizationLimits: Short source-led conversation exception, not a full-recipe pass. No failed effort or inward turning scene is invented.

The distinct early 1864 learning-and-criticism episode replaces the 1862–1866 accusation/acquittal stage. Approximate ages 19–20 follow the museum birth-year anchor and Child's contemporary description, not a known exact birthday.
No poisoning-case chronology, assault, expulsion, college motive or causal route from injustice to art is asserted.
An invitation to inspect a bust is not an accomplished studio visit or received criticism. No historical quotes or texture.
avoidRules: Do not repeat the source writer's racial hierarchy or endorse praise based on race.
Do not promise success, fair treatment or improvement to the reader.

arc.canonicalText: A writer met her at a reception and asked about her sculpture. She was about twenty.
arc.sourceNote: A contemporary reported conversation, not a reconstructed studio visit. Child supplied approximate age; metadata19–20 reflects the museum1844 anchor, not an exact known birthday.

arc.canonicalText: She told the writer that some people praised her because she was Black. That was not the kind of praise she wanted.
arc.sourceNote: STRUCTURAL EXCEPTION: expressed objection in the same conversation, not a fabricated low or humiliation scene. Child's own condescending framing is not adopted as truth.

arc.canonicalText: She described how she had gone to an established sculptor for advice. He had made a bust of an abolitionist. She thought he might be a friend to her people.
arc.sourceNote: An explicitly recounted earlier action, not a claim that this followed the reception or an invented cause from the poisoning case. Names withheld until identity bridge.

arc.canonicalText: She had made a first bust by copying another sculpted head. She said that praise was not good for her.
arc.sourceNote: STRUCTURAL EXCEPTION: her objection to unhelpful praise, not an assessment that the bust was bad or an invented failed trial.

arc.canonicalText: She invited the writer to visit her room and look at the bust. She asked her to point out its faults.
arc.sourceNote: The invitation and request are reported; no completed visit, supplied criticism or resulting revision is asserted.

arc.canonicalText: She said that hearing about the faults would teach her something. She had also spoken of the sculptor's kindness. She wanted useful criticism.
arc.sourceNote: Limited endpoint is her stated wish in the conversation, not proof of improvement, later success or emotional transformation.

arc.canonicalText:
Her name was Edmonia Lewis.

She was a sculptor who made portraits in marble.

Your life is not theirs. But a piece of this story may still sit beside you.

You are allowed to want useful feedback.
arc.sourceNote: Own-line identity reveal and non-prescriptive permission.
